@graph.headline: The Alternate Valuation Date for Digital Assets: IRC Section 2032, Dual-Date Appraisal Requirements, and Why Crypto Volatility Changes the Estate Tax Analysis
@graph.description: The Section 2032 alternate valuation date election is the only federal lever an executor has when a digital asset portfolio falls after death. This practitioner-level analysis covers the statute, the included-versus-excluded property distinction for staking rewards and airdrops, the marital and charitable deduction adjustment that quietly erodes the benefit, dual-date appraisal scope, and the procedural deadlines that govern a missed election.

about.name: IRC Section 2032 Alternate Valuation Date for Digital Assets
about.description: The alternate valuation election under IRC Section 2032 applied to cryptocurrency, NFT, and other digital asset holdings in a decedent's gross estate. Covers the three valuation dates of Section 2032(a), the all-or-nothing rule of Treasury Regulation 20.2032-1(b)(1), the double-decrease test of Section 2032(c), the election and revocation mechanics of Section 2032(d), the one-year filing limitation, the last-day-of-the-sixth-month rule of Rev. Rul. 74-260, the included property versus excluded property distinction of Regulation 20.2032-1(d) as applied to staking rewards, DeFi yield, airdrops, and hard fork proceeds under Rev. Rul. 2023-14 and Rev. Rul. 2019-24, the treatment of sales, token migrations, and in-kind distributions inside the six-month window under Regulation 20.2032-1(c), the adjustment of the Section 2056 marital deduction and Section 2055 charitable deduction under Regulation 20.2032-1(g), the basis consequence under Section 1014(a) and the consistency reporting framework of Section 1014(f) and Section 6035, penalty exposure under Section 6662 and the appraiser penalty under Section 6695A, dual-date USPAP Standards 7 and 9 appraisal scope, Form 706 Part III line 1 election mechanics, Schedule F reporting of digital assets, protective elections under Regulation 20.2032-1(b)(2), and Section 301.9100 relief for a missed election as granted in PLR 202513003, PLR 202410006, PLR 202425012, and PLR-108574-11.

mainEntity.name: What is the alternate valuation date for digital assets?

acceptedAnswer.text: It is the date six months after death, or the date an asset was distributed, sold, exchanged, or otherwise disposed of if that occurred earlier. Under IRC Section 2032 it applies to the entire gross estate, not to digital assets alone. Where no numerically corresponding date exists in the sixth month, the last day of that month governs under Rev. Rul. 74-260.

mainEntity.name: Does electing the alternate valuation date reduce the heirs' step-up in basis?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. Under Section 1014(a), elective alternate valuation makes the applicable valuation date the beneficiary's basis, so a lower alternate value produces a lower step-up and a larger gain on a later sale. Where the estate tax savings are modest relative to the basis reduction, the election can be net-negative.

mainEntity.name: How are staking rewards and airdrops received during the six-month window treated?

acceptedAnswer.text: As excluded property under Treasury Regulation 20.2032-1(d). They are earned or accrued after death, so they are not added to the alternate-date gross estate. They are income when received, generally at fair market value on the receipt date under the principles of Rev. Rul. 2023-14 and Rev. Rul. 2019-24, and that value becomes basis.

mainEntity.name: What happens if the executor sells crypto within six months of death?

acceptedAnswer.text: The disposed-of asset is valued as of the disposition date under Section 2032(a)(1), not the six-month date. A conversion, a distribution to a beneficiary, or a sale to fund administration expenses therefore fixes the valuation date for that asset and can lock in a low value.

mainEntity.name: Do you need two appraisals to support a Form 706 alternate valuation election?

acceptedAnswer.text: You need valuation conclusions at both dates. That means date-of-death fair market value for every asset, which is required in any event to test Section 2032(c) and to preserve the fallback position described in C.C.A. 201926013, plus alternate-date value or value at the disposition date for the assets actually reported at the alternate date. A single dual-date engagement is the efficient way to produce both.

mainEntity.name: Can the alternate valuation election be made after Form 706 has been filed?

acceptedAnswer.text: The election must be made by the executor on the return, but Section 2032(d)(2) permits it on a return filed up to one year after the due date including extensions, and the Service has granted Section 301.9100 relief where the return was filed without the election and an amended or supplemental return followed within that period. Treasury Regulation 20.2032-1(b)(3) forecloses relief beyond that limit.

mainEntity.name: Who decides whether to make the alternate valuation election, the executor or the IRS?

acceptedAnswer.text: The executor decides, on the return. The IRS determines on examination whether the statutory conditions were in fact met, and under C.C.A. 201926013 the date-of-death values must be used if adjustments show the election did not decrease both the gross estate and the combined estate and GST tax.

mainEntity.name: Is a qualified appraisal required for estate tax purposes?

acceptedAnswer.text: The qualified appraisal requirement of IRS Section 170(f)(11) governs charitable contribution substantiation rather than Form 706 as such. Estate valuation is nonetheless tested against Section 6662 valuation misstatement thresholds, and appraisers face separate exposure under Section 6695A, so a USPAP-compliant appraisal supported by defensible data is the professional standard for any concentrated digital position, and is mandatory in substance where the estate also claims a charitable deduction for digital assets.
